kind: lab measurement (ChainLab, simulation from the drivers' source)
question: Does a drop-check memory that stays armed through queued report bursts (plugin 1.4, DropCheck 2) beat the 1.3 memory, and what does it cost on the shipped drop / late grid?
method: AimForge --burst-lab. 8 cards (goat, bo6og, breakpoint, breakwide, rivpsy, owsol, valmp, apxmp) x 4 ChainLab scenarios x 3 seeds. Timing.Burst: Poisson host stalls of 3-8 ms; every report arriving during a stall is released when it ends, back to back. Metric: aim error per 100 ms window (degrees), mean over all rows. Drop/Late grid: every 3rd to 17th report dropped or late.

dropLateGrid.where: breakpoint tap band 12mm 1.2Hz Drop every 3 seed 1: 0.0379 -> 0.0392

conclusion: With queued bursts the 1.4 memory holds the no-stall floor at every stall rate tested, where 1.3 degrades from 2 stalls/s on. On the drop/late grid it is the same or better on all but a handful of rows at one report in three dropped, where it gives back about a thousandth of a degree (an armed check can misjudge a real drop while the hand decelerates). DropCheck 2 is the apply default; a 1.3 plugin reads 2 as 1.
limits: Simulation. The stall rate of the real rig under real game load is not known; the Hand Print recorder counts it (gap classes) from plugin 1.4 on.
